paras: The killing of Julian Jones was the fatal shooting of a Black farm hand by Raleigh policeman William E. Hogue on Hargett street in Raleigh, North Carolina, on August 2, 1890. Hogue, who said he fired while making an arrest, was charged with murder on a Black man's warrant, jailed without bail and indicted in September. Black residents packed the hearings, and the city kept its militia company ready.

Jones, about forty-five, worked on Mr. Goodwin's farm outside the city and, according to the News and Observer, had been drinking in town that Saturday. On Wilmington street he knocked down a white man named Frazier, who the State Chronicle said had cursed him, and then struck William Utley, who tried to part them.

Hogue tried to arrest Jones near Hargett street, was knocked to his knees and lost his club, though the papers disagreed over whether Jones took it. As Jones ran up Hargett street, Hogue fired two shots, one of which wounded Furman Betts, a white bystander, in the thigh. Hogue then caught Jones and fired a third shot at close range into his abdomen, and Jones died within minutes. City authorities judged an inquest unnecessary and gave the body to his friends.

A Black man, William Jones, swore out a murder warrant before Justice M. B. Barbee, who held hearings on August 2, 4 and 5 and committed Hogue to jail without bail for murder. The Richmond Times reported that Black churches took collections to hire prosecutors and that a Black lawyer appeared for the prosecution. The Governor's Guard slept in its armory on the first two nights, and the aldermen voted $150 to equip it because of what the Times called "bad blood" among Black residents.

Hogue's counsel decided not to seek habeas corpus. A grand jury indicted him for murder on September 23, but Judge E. T. Boykin's illness adjourned the court before trial, and the case went over to the next criminal term. No report of a verdict appears in the coverage through September.

Hogue said he fired only after being struck and disarmed, and the State Chronicle reported his claim that bystanders cried "shoot him, shoot him." Other eyewitnesses told the Chronicle that Jones was trying to get away when Hogue held him and fired. At the hearing, Black witnesses Philip Harris, Nick Blount and William Green testified that Hogue shot Jones while holding him, and Green said Jones cried for help and Hogue answered with a curse and "I'll help you." White defense witnesses said Jones turned and struck at the officer, some with something in his hand, and a city worker produced a knife he said he found near the scene two days later.

A short wire dispatch ran on August 3 in Washington, Richmond and Savannah papers, and in Asheville the next day. Its fuller form said Jones had Hogue's club and was about to use it, under headlines such as "A Desperate Darkey" and "A Bad Negro Slain." The News and Observer headed its report "An Obstreperous Negro," yet its editorial doubted the officer's right to fire on a retreating man and insisted race made the offense "neither greater nor less."

Both Raleigh dailies printed the hearing testimony at length, and both raised an old killing by Hogue's father, which the Chronicle then regretted mentioning. The Richmond Times wrote of Black crowds who "murmer ominously" and later were "in high glee" at the commitment, and a Winston correspondent reported anger there at the murder charge. A Winston reprint of the Chronicle's account named the dead man "James Jones," and no Black-press account was found.

reader.title: Killing of Julian Jones
bases: A single Raleigh policeman, William E. Hogue, shot Jones while trying to arrest him after a street fight; no mob or posse did the killing (A3, A8).

Two independent Raleigh dailies, a Richmond Times special and the AP-type wire agree that Hogue shot and killed Jones on Hargett street on August 2 (A1, A3, A4, A8); only the circumstances of the fatal shot are disputed.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Jones knocked down a white man, then in a scuffle got Hogue's club and was about to use it when Hogue fired three times, the last shot fatal.

accounts.label: Officer Hogue
accounts.gist: He fired only after being struck and disarmed of his club, to make the arrest; bystanders cried 'shoot him'; he could not say whether Jones had the club.

accounts.label: Black prosecution witnesses
accounts.gist: Hogue caught Jones, held him and shot him in the stomach while Jones was doing nothing; Jones cried for help and Hogue cursed him.

accounts.label: White defense witnesses
accounts.gist: Jones halted, turned and grappled with or struck at Hogue, possibly with something in his hand, before the last shot; a knife was found two days later near the scene.

accounts.label: Unnamed eyewitnesses
accounts.gist: Jones was not fighting but trying to get away when Hogue held him with one arm and fired.

framing.detail: Wire headlines 'A Desperate Darkey' and 'A Bad Negro Slain. He Was About to Club a Policeman When Shot.'
News and Observer called Jones 'obstreperous' and 'lawless' but doubted the officer's right to fire on a retreating man and left the matter to the court.
State Chronicle printed conflicting eyewitness accounts and full testimony, while its Winston correspondent relayed denunciation of the murder commitment.
Richmond Times headlined 'Negro Killed While Resisting an Officer' and centered Black crowds' 'ominous' mood and 'glee'.

conflicts.note: The Western Sentinel reprint (A20) has 'James Jones'; the Raleigh indictment reports use Julian.
